transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-08-01
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 min
Recording: enabled
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Mark (Redwood SE), James (Cortexly CTO), Sofia (Eng Mgr), Liam (Platform Eng)

Summary:
Quick demo/walkthrough focused on edge cases: very long context windows, sustained high TPS, streaming backpressure and timeouts. Covered Redwood API, Console, and Redwood Optimize recommendations plus Dedicated options and POC plan. Agreed to run a dedicated benchmark and share artifacts.

Topics:
- Long context support (100k+ tokens, KV cache behavior)
- High TPS (sustained 500-2k TPS per endpoint)
- Streaming backpressure and chunking, client reconnects and timeouts
- Autoscaling and Dedicated capacity tradeoffs
- Observability and alerts (p95/p99 latency, queue depth, token cost)

-- Transcript body --
[00:00:00] Alex: hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intros, i'm alex, i'm the AE on the account. priya and mark from the se side will run the deep bits.
[00:00:12] James: yeah hi, james here. thanks, short on time so appreciate a focused demo. our key two concerns are long context and then the sheer TPS we need during peak, and we get weird timeouts on streaming if clients buffer.
[00:00:28] Priya: great, that's exactly what we planned. we'll show the api behavior, console observability, and then our optimize suggestions for batching/caching and quantization. note, some words from the recording may be off — the transcript engine sometimes swaps redwood dedcated for dedicated.
[00:00:45] Mark: quick note on sizing: when you say high TPS, what's your ballpark? previously you mentioned 1k sustained per endpoint, right?
[00:00:55] Sofia: correct, 800–1,200 sustained during business hours, spikes to ~3k for a few minutes on heavy events. single tenant, private data, so VPC constraints apply.
[00:01:10] Alex: ok, good. so we'll run through three demos: 1) long context end-to-end (console + api), 2) synthetic TPS load and how routing/queues act, 3) streaming with backpressure and timeout handling.
[00:01:25] Priya: starting long-context demo: we have a model shard with extended kv-cache support. note that for extremely long prefix retention we recommend 4 things: pin the model version, enable persistent KV cache (we call it prefix caching), configure windowed attention if you need sliding summaries, and use optimized quantization profile to keep memory stable.
[00:01:50] James: can you show the console and the API call? and how latency behaves as context grows?
[00:01:57] Priya: yeah — console: you can see token usage, cache hit rate, and per-request kv cache size. (screen share) here, p50 remains low until about 64k tokens, p95 climbs as we start hitting cross-host kv fetch. we show 'cache miss rate' spike at around 96k because of chunking.
[00:02:20] [00:02:20] Sofia: hmm, our use case often needs 120k of context, does that map?
[00:02:25] Priya: it can. for 120k we recommend either: 1) reserved Dedicated pool with larger KV memory (pins), or 2) an approach where you summarize and stitch the context in the client to keep active sequence length lower. Redwood Optimize can generate summary templates to keep salient facts without holding raw 120k each call.
[00:02:45] Mark: also note that the runtime will transparently fall back to chunked KV fetches — that increases latency but keeps throughput steady. you can configure fallback policies in the routing layer (e.g., prefer lower-latency model variant or increase timeout).
[00:03:05] [00:03:05] James: what about cost? holding prefix cache for long sessions seems expensive.
[00:03:10] Alex: yes, cost tradeoff — Optimize will estimate token-equivalent cost and recommend quantization + cache eviction policy. usually Dedicated pool pricing gives you predictable unit costs vs hosted ephemeral bursts. we'll include numbers in the benchmark spreadsheet.
[00:03:28] Priya: switching to TPS demo — we ran a synthetic load earlier. on hosted API with autoscaling, the router does request routing by policy; for sustained 1k TPS we observed steady p50 ~90ms, p95 ~260ms, p99 ~480ms for a medium-sized model. under spikes to 3k, queueing increased and we saw backpressure.
[00:03:55] Liam: in our infra we use long-lived gRPC streams for clients. streaming backpressure tends to cause client timeouts when the server can't keep up with chunk delivery. what specific knobs do we expose?
[00:04:08] Priya: two main levers: server-side chunk size / rate limit and client-side backoff. in the API we have streaming chunk envelope settings and backpressure-aware dispatch. you'll also want to use our circuit-breaker and retry policy — for streaming we prefer resumable streams (a tokenized continuation) rather than naive reconnects.
[00:04:28] Mark: specifically, we expose: 1) streaming chunk max bytes and target chunk interval, 2) per-connection token quota, 3) queue depth thresholds and automatic spillover to a fallback model or delayed callback. we also emit a 'streaming.backpressure' metric you can alert on.
[00:04:45] [00:04:45] Sofia: any hard timeouts on the hosted side? we've had clients with 30s HTTP timeouts.
[00:04:52] Alex: default request timeout is 60s on the hosted API, but you can set client-side timeouts shorter. for streaming, we recommend keep-alive pings and using the resumable stream approach; if a connection drops mid-stream the client can resume from last acknowledged token.
[00:05:10] James: what if it still fails, we need graceful degradation — return a short summary or fall back to a smaller model?
[00:05:16] Priya: yes, fallback policies are first-class: canary to cheaper model, degrade to summary-only responses, or return cached completion if available. console lets you configure automatic fallback thresholds (e.g., if queue depth > 80% for >30s, route to fallback model).
[00:05:33] Mark: demoing the streaming backpressure simulator (shared link to load tool and logs) — you'll see simulated client network slowness and server queue growth; the system applies backpressure and then triggers our spillover policy. (screen) logs show streaming.chunk_delay metrics and the system cuts chunk size to recover.
[00:05:55] [00:05:55] James: nice. can you share the synthetic load results? we want p99 numbers at our target TPS.
[00:06:00] Alex: yes, we'll share the spreadsheet. summary from earlier runs: medium model, hosted autoscale: 1k sustained -> p99 ~480ms; dedicated with 4x GPUs & pinned KV -> p99 ~220ms. costs differ by ~2.5x but predictability improves.
[00:06:18] Sofia: that's helpful. security/compliance — we are regulated, need SOC2, SAML SSO, audit logs, and KMS integration. can you confirm private deployment options?
[00:06:27] Alex: absolutely. Private deployment supports customer VPC, KMS/HSM integration, and audit logs; we have a compliance pack and will share SOC 2 and ISO docs. POC can run in a private VPC if needed.
[00:06:40] Priya: one more technical note: for long context retention we recommend quantization profiles that preserve KV pointer stability; avoid ultra aggressive quant that can add decode jitter. Optimize will recommend the right profile per workload.
[00:06:54] [00:06:54] Liam: for the POC, what infra do you need from our side?
[00:06:58] Priya: we'll need sample traffic (trace), examples of long-context documents, and a small test harness that exercises streaming clients. if you want private POC, IAM role and a VPC peering or a small on-prem artifact package. we'll include exact checklist.
[00:07:12] Alex: wrapping up — quick recap and next steps. we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and synthetic run logs; priya will share the POC checklist; cortexly to send sample traffic and confirm security contacts. schedule kickoff for week of 8/10.
[00:07:30] James: thanks everyone, that sounds good.
